body_es: `git push` envía los commits que existen localmente pero no en el repositorio remoto, actualizando la rama remota correspondiente para que apunte al mismo commit que tu rama local. Por defecto empuja la rama actual a la rama remota con el mismo nombre, siempre que tengas permisos de escritura sobre el repositorio. La condición clave es que Git solo acepta un push cuando la rama remota es un prefijo exacto de tu historial local, es decir, cuando tu rama local simplemente le añade commits encima: eso permite mover el puntero remoto sin perder trabajo de nadie. Si otra persona ya subió commits que tú no tienes, la rama remota dejó de ser un prefijo de la tuya y Git rechaza el push con un error de "non-fast-forward", obligándote a traer esos cambios primero con `git pull` (o `fetch` y `merge`/`rebase`) antes de reintentar. Por ejemplo, empujar un commit nuevo sobre una rama remota que aún no lo tiene produce una actualización limpia mostrando el rango de commits movido; empujar contra una rama remota que avanzó con un commit distinto produce el rechazo. `git push -u origin <rama>` además vincula la rama local con la remota para que futuros `push`/`pull` no necesiten especificarlas. Un error común es usar `git push --force` para forzar la actualización tras un rechazo sin entender por qué ocurrió, lo que puede borrar commits ajenos del historial remoto.
body_en: `git push` sends the commits that exist locally but not in the remote repository, updating the corresponding remote branch so it points to the same commit as your local branch. By default it pushes the current branch to the remote branch with the same name, as long as you have write permissions on the repository. The key condition is that Git only accepts a push when the remote branch is an exact prefix of your local history, meaning your local branch simply adds commits on top of it: that lets the remote pointer move without losing anyone's work. If someone else already pushed commits you do not have, the remote branch is no longer a prefix of yours and Git rejects the push with a "non-fast-forward" error, forcing you to pull those changes first (via `git pull`, or `fetch` and `merge`/`rebase`) before trying again. For example, pushing a new commit onto a remote branch that does not yet have it produces a clean update showing the range of commits moved; pushing against a remote branch that advanced with a different commit produces the rejection. `git push -u origin <branch>` also links the local branch with the remote one so future `push`/`pull` commands do not need to specify them. A common mistake is using `git push --force` to force the update after a rejection without understanding why it happened, which can erase other people's commits from the remote history.
example_code:
local_master = ["a1b2c3d", "5b3c2d1", "7x8y9z0"]
remote_master = ["a1b2c3d", "5b3c2d1"]

def push(local, remote, branch):
    if remote == local[:len(remote)]:
        new_commits = local[len(remote):]
        old_tip = remote[-1][:7] if remote else "0000000"
        new_tip = local[-1][:7]
        print(f"Writing objects: 100% ({len(new_commits)}/{len(new_commits)}), done.")
        print("To https://github.com/user/repo.git")
        print(f"   {old_tip}..{new_tip}  {branch} -> {branch}")
        return list(local)
    print(f"! [rejected]        {branch} -> {branch} (non-fast-forward)")
    print("error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/user/repo.git'")
    return remote

remote_master = push(local_master, remote_master, "master")

diverged_remote = ["a1b2c3d", "5b3c2d1", "9z8y7x6"]
push(local_master, diverged_remote, "master")
